note: Records of the reference-checked analysis methods in analysis_methods.py, in the shape of packages/domain/src/method-records.json. `dependencies` are the runtime image's pins (deploy/runtime-dsh/install-runtime.sh, held equal by a test); a result also reports the versions it actually ran on. `version` changes when the method's numbers, inputs, checks or diagnostics change; a result carries it with the record's digest and the digest of the module. Only strings, integers and booleans appear here. `seeded: false` means the method draws no random numbers.

compare_groups.title: Comparison of a continuous outcome between two groups: Welch or Student t test, paired t test, Mann-Whitney test
compare_groups.estimand: The difference between the two groups' mean outcomes (first minus second, named in the result), with a 95% interval for the t tests; the Mann-Whitney test reports its statistic and p value only.

assumptions.text: Each row is one independent subject. A person with several rows, or in both groups, breaks independence.
The t tests assume the group means are approximately normal (large enough groups or a roughly normal outcome); Welch's test does not assume equal variances.
Rows with a missing value are dropped, which is only harmless when the values are missing at random with respect to the outcome.

The groups are comparable apart from the exposure; randomization, or adjustment, is not provided here. A covariate that differs between the groups by more than a tenth of a standard deviation is named.
The difference is first minus second; a contrast is named by the caller or the direction is inferred and said so.
A p value is for one prespecified comparison; several comparisons need an adjustment.

inputs.name: groups
inputs.range: exactly two distinct labels after dropping missing

inputs.name: contrast
inputs.range: optional; the two labels, first minus second

inputs.name: subject
inputs.range: optional; names the person of each row

inputs.name: aggregate_subjects
inputs.range: optional; compare each person's mean when persons have several rows

inputs.name: covariates
inputs.range: optional; one row per row of values

refusals.when: the data do not hold exactly two groups, or the contrast names a group that is not there
a person appears in both groups: the data are paired, and an independent-groups test would count each person twice
a person has several rows in one group: repeated measurements are not independent; use aggregate_subjects or a model for repeated measures
a paired test was asked for and the rows do not form one pair per person
a group has fewer than two observations
the outcome does not vary, so the t statistic is undefined

diagnostics.when: rows with a missing outcome, group or predictor were dropped (listwise); the counts say how many
the share of rows dropped differs by more than ten percentage points between groups, so the missing values may not be ignorable
no contrast was named, so the difference is the first label in sorted order minus the second
each person's mean replaced their rows (aggregate_subjects)
a group has fewer than ten observations: normality cannot be examined and the t test leans on it
one group is more than three times the other
a covariate's standardized difference between the groups exceeds 0.1
the Mann-Whitney test does not test the difference in means that is reported alongside it
the caller said this is one of several tests (family_size above 1) and no adjustment was applied; adjust_pvalues does it

references.source: Student (1908) / Cushny & Peebles (1905) sleep data as printed in R's ?t.test: Welch t -1.8608 on 17.776 df, p 0.07939, interval -3.3655 to 0.2055; paired t -4.0621 on 9 df, p 0.002833, interval -2.4599 to -0.7001; Wilcoxon W 25.5, p 0.06933

covariate_balance.title: Standardized mean difference of covariates between two groups
covariate_balance.estimand: For each covariate, (mean of the first group minus mean of the second) over the root mean of the two variances (Austin 2009). An absolute value above 0.1 is imbalance.

assumptions.text: 0.1 is a convention for noticing imbalance, not a test; a smaller difference in a covariate that drives the outcome can still confound.
Only the covariates supplied are examined; an unmeasured confounder is not.

inputs.name: covariates
inputs.range: one row per row of groups; binary covariates are coded 0/1

refusals.when: the data do not hold exactly two groups

diagnostics.when: some covariate's absolute standardized difference exceeds 0.1

references.source: hand-computed standardized differences on small tables, and the formula of Austin (2009), Statistics in Medicine 28:3083

contingency_test.title: Association in a table of counts: Pearson chi-square, Fisher exact test, odds ratio, risk ratio, risk difference
contingency_test.estimand: For a 2 x 2 table (rows groups, first column the event): the odds ratio with Woolf and exact conditional intervals, the risk ratio, the risk difference and the p values of Pearson's, Yates' and Fisher's tests; for a larger table, Pearson's chi-square and Cramer's V.

assumptions.text: Each subject is counted once. Repeated or paired observations in a table (a before-and-after count) need McNemar's test, not this.
Pearson's chi-square needs expected counts of about 5 or more; below that the exact test is the primary one for a 2 x 2 table.
A ratio from a table with a zero cell is not estimable; a continuity correction is an explicit choice, and it is named when made.
A crude table does not adjust for a third variable; a stratified or regression analysis does.
A p value is for one prespecified table.

inputs.name: table
inputs.range: two or more rows and columns, each count 0 or more

refusals.when: the table is not a rectangle of non-negative whole numbers
a row or a column of the table has no counts at all

diagnostics.when: an expected cell count is below 5: Pearson's chi-square is unreliable
the table holds fewer than 20 subjects
a cell is 0, so the odds and risk ratios are not given; the exact and chi-square tests still are
0.5 was added to every cell to give the ratios (correct_zero_cells)
the caller said this is one of several tests (family_size above 1) and no adjustment was applied; adjust_pvalues does it

references.source: Fisher's lady tasting tea (Fisher 1935): table 3, 1, 1, 3; two-sided exact p 34/70 = 0.4857, as printed in R's ?fisher.test; conditional odds ratio 6.4083
references.tolerance: exact fraction; 1e-5 relative for the odds ratio

references.source: Physicians' Health Study (NEJM 1989) 2 x 2 table: Pearson chi-square 25.01 and odds ratio 1.832 (1.440, 2.331) as printed in Agresti; Yates 24.429 from R chisq.test
Agresti, Categorical Data Analysis, party identification by gender (women 762, 327, 468; men 484, 239, 477): Pearson chi-square 30.1 on 2 df

linear_regression.title: Ordinary least squares with an intercept, with cluster-robust standard errors for repeated measurements
linear_regression.estimand: The change in the mean outcome per unit of each predictor, holding the others fixed, with t-based 95% intervals and p values.

assumptions.text: The mean outcome is linear in the predictors as entered.
Rows are independent. A person with several rows is a cluster: the standard errors are cluster-robust (CR1, t with clusters - 1 df) unless the caller insists on independence.
The error variance does not change with the predictors; the Breusch-Pagan test notices when it does.
The predictors are not collinear and there are more observations than parameters.
About ten observations per parameter keep the fit from over-reading noise.
No handful of rows decides the fit; Cook's distance above 4/n counts the candidates.

inputs.name: X
inputs.range: one row per row of y; an intercept is added

inputs.name: subject
inputs.range: optional; repeated rows of one person become one cluster

refusals.when: not more observations (or clusters) than parameters
the predictors are linearly dependent, so the coefficients are not identified

diagnostics.when: rows with a missing outcome, group or predictor were dropped (listwise); the counts say how many
a person has several rows and the caller asked for independent rows anyway
standard errors are cluster-robust because persons have several rows
fewer than ten observations per parameter
a variance inflation factor exceeds 10
the Breusch-Pagan test rejects constant variance at 0.05
some rows have a Cook's distance above 4/n
the caller said this is one of several tests (family_size above 1) and no adjustment was applied; adjust_pvalues does it

references.source: NIST Statistical Reference Datasets, Longley (an ill-conditioned fit with six predictors): certified coefficients, standard errors, residual standard deviation and R-squared to 15 digits

logistic_regression.title: Logistic regression of a binary outcome by maximum likelihood, with Wald intervals and odds ratios
logistic_regression.estimand: The log odds ratio of the event per unit of each predictor, holding the others fixed, reported with odds ratios and Wald 95% intervals.

assumptions.text: The log odds are linear in the predictors as entered.
Rows are independent; repeated measurements get cluster-robust standard errors.
The maximum likelihood estimate exists: no predictor combination separates events from non-events, the predictors are not collinear, and the outcome takes both values.
About ten events (and non-events) per predictor keep the fit from over-reading noise.
The outcome is 0 or 1 with 1 the event.

inputs.name: X
inputs.range: one row per row of y; an intercept is added

refusals.when: the outcome holds values other than 0 and 1
every row has the same outcome, so there is nothing to model
the predictors are linearly dependent
a combination of the predictors perfectly or almost perfectly separates events from non-events: the maximum likelihood estimate does not exist
the fit did not converge

diagnostics.when: rows with a missing outcome, group or predictor were dropped (listwise); the counts say how many
fewer than ten events or non-events per predictor
a person has several rows and the caller asked for independent rows anyway
standard errors are cluster-robust because persons have several rows
the caller said this is one of several tests (family_size above 1) and no adjustment was applied; adjust_pvalues does it

references.source: Agresti, Categorical Data Analysis, snoring and heart disease (2,484 subjects, scores 0, 2, 4, 5): logit = -3.866 + 0.397 x, standard errors 0.166 and 0.050; the fit also run in R 4.3.3 glm()
references.tolerance: three printed decimals; 1e-6 relative against R

references.source: R 4.3.3 glm(binomial) of death on age and sex in the survival package's lung data

kaplan_meier.title: Kaplan-Meier survival curve with Greenwood standard errors and the median survival time
kaplan_meier.estimand: The probability of remaining event-free beyond each event time, per group, with a 95% band (log scale by default, as R's survfit) and the median survival time with its interval.

assumptions.text: Censoring is unrelated to the prognosis: a subject censored at a time has the same outlook as those who stay.
The event indicator is 1 for the event and 0 for censored; nothing else is guessed.
There are no competing events that preclude the event of interest; with competing risks 1 - KM overstates the incidence.
Every subject enters at time 0 (no delayed entry) and is followed until the event or right censoring.
The curve's tail rests on the few subjects still at risk.

refusals.when: no row has a time, an event indicator and every covariate
the event indicator holds values other than 0 and 1, so which value is the event is not known
a follow-up time is negative

diagnostics.when: rows with a missing outcome, group or predictor were dropped (listwise); the counts say how many
the share of rows dropped differs by more than ten percentage points between groups, so the missing values may not be ignorable
more than half the subjects are censored: the tail of the curve rests on few events
fewer than ten events: estimates are unstable
several events share a time; the tie-handling method matters (Efron is used unless Breslow is asked for)
some subjects have a follow-up time of exactly 0 and contribute nothing
a group has no events, so its curve is flat at 1
fewer than ten subjects remain at risk at the last event time
the curve never falls to 0.5, so there is no median (the curve itself is complete)

references.source: Miller (1981) acute myelogenous leukaemia data (R's survival::aml): median 31 weeks (95% 18 to not reached) maintained and 23 (8 to not reached) not maintained, as printed in the survival package
North Central Cancer Treatment Group lung cancer data (survival::lung): median 310 days (95% 285 to 363), as printed in the survival package's documentation and tutorials

log_rank.title: Log-rank test of equal hazards across groups, optionally stratified
log_rank.estimand: Whether the groups' hazard functions are equal over follow-up (chi-square on groups - 1 degrees of freedom). It is a test, not an effect size.

assumptions.text: Censoring is unrelated to the prognosis.
The test is valid whatever the hazards do, but most powerful when they are proportional; crossing curves can give a nonsignificant result for a real difference.
The event indicator is 1 for the event and 0 for censored.
Each row is a different subject.

refusals.when: no row has a time, an event indicator and every covariate
the event indicator holds values other than 0 and 1, so which value is the event is not known
a follow-up time is negative
there is only one group, so nothing to compare
no subject has the event
the variance of the statistic is singular (for example every event happens at one time with one subject per group at risk), so the statistic is not defined

diagnostics.when: rows with a missing outcome, group or predictor were dropped (listwise); the counts say how many
the share of rows dropped differs by more than ten percentage points between groups, so the missing values may not be ignorable
more than half the subjects are censored: the tail of the curve rests on few events
fewer than ten events: estimates are unstable
several events share a time; the tie-handling method matters (Efron is used unless Breslow is asked for)
some subjects have a follow-up time of exactly 0 and contribute nothing

references.source: survival::aml maintained against not maintained: log-rank chi-square 3.4 on 1 df, p 0.0653, as printed in the survival package's ?survdiff
survival::lung by sex: log-rank chi-square 10.3 on 1 df, p 0.00131, observed 112 and 53 against expected 91.6 and 73.4

cox_regression.title: Cox proportional hazards regression with Efron or Breslow ties, a likelihood-ratio test and a proportional-hazards test
cox_regression.estimand: The log hazard ratio of the event per unit of each covariate, holding the others fixed, reported as hazard ratios with Wald 95% intervals.

assumptions.text: A covariate's hazard ratio is constant over follow-up. The score test of a time-varying coefficient (R's cox.zph) questions this; a large p value does not establish it.
Censoring is unrelated to the prognosis.
Each row is a different subject; clustered rows get cluster-robust standard errors.
Covariates are not collinear, there are more events than covariates, and a binary covariate has events at both levels.
About ten events per covariate keep the fit from over-reading noise.
A continuous covariate acts linearly on the log hazard as entered.
Every subject is at risk from time 0; left truncation and time-varying covariates are not supported.

inputs.name: X
inputs.range: one row per row of time

refusals.when: no row has a time, an event indicator and every covariate
the event indicator holds values other than 0 and 1, so which value is the event is not known
a follow-up time is negative
no subject has the event
not more events than covariates
the covariates are linearly dependent
a binary covariate has no events at one of its levels, so its hazard ratio is infinite or zero
the partial likelihood did not give finite estimates

diagnostics.when: rows with a missing outcome, group or predictor were dropped (listwise); the counts say how many
more than half the subjects are censored: the tail of the curve rests on few events
fewer than ten events: estimates are unstable
several events share a time; the tie-handling method matters (Efron is used unless Breslow is asked for)
some subjects have a follow-up time of exactly 0 and contribute nothing
fewer than ten events per covariate
standard errors are cluster-robust because subjects have several rows
the score test of a time-varying coefficient rejects proportional hazards for a covariate at 0.05
the assumption test is not run for a stratified or cluster-robust fit
the caller said this is one of several tests (family_size above 1) and no adjustment was applied; adjust_pvalues does it

references.source: survival::lung, coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex): age 0.017045 (se 0.009223, z 1.848, p 0.06459), sex -0.513219 (se 0.167458, z -3.065, p 0.00218), likelihood-ratio 14.12 on 2 df, as printed in the survival package's documentation and tutorials

R 4.3.3 survival 3.5-8: Breslow coefficients 0.01701289 and -0.51256479, and cox.zph (transform km) chi-square 0.2092 (age), 2.6077 (sex) and 2.7708 (global) for Efron ties, 0.2080, 2.5995 and 2.7610 for Breslow

adjust_pvalues.title: Multiplicity adjustment of p values: Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg
adjust_pvalues.estimand: Adjusted p values in the order given: Bonferroni and Holm control the family-wise error rate, Benjamini-Hochberg the false discovery rate.

assumptions.text: The adjusted family is the set of p values passed in; choosing which tests count is the researcher's, and omitting some inflates the error rate.
Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate for independent or positively dependent tests.

refusals.when: no p values, a missing one, or one outside 0 to 1

references.source: Benjamini & Hochberg (1995) JRSS B 57:289, the 15 p values of the worked example: the procedure at q = 0.05 rejects the four smallest
R 4.3.3 p.adjust(method = 'holm' / 'BH' / 'bonferroni') on the same 15 p values
